title: Exponential logical-error reduction in quantum memories via optimal syndrome-measurement timing
authors: Tobias Haug, Kishor Bharti, Leandro Aolita
abstract: Syndrome-measurements timing is usually treated as a fixed clock cycle of a quantum error-correcting code. For quantum memories, however, the intra-measurement interval is itself an optimizable control parameter: measuring too rarely allows idling errors to accumulate, whereas measuring too often introduces measurement-induced faults. We propose a phenomenological logical-noise model for this trade-off and analytically show that the optimal syndrome-measurements interval scales inversely proportionally with the code distance and that this produces an exponential reduction of logical-error rates in the distance relative to constant-interval schedules. Furthermore, for time-dependent idling noise, we develop an adaptive timing strategy based on the measured syndrome activity that outperforms every fixed-interval protocol, with largest gains for short but strong noise bursts. Simulations of rotated surface-code memories with matching decoding validate the phenomenological model, the distance-dependent optimum, and the adaptive-strategy improvement. Moreover, with the experimental noise parameters reported by Google in Nature 638 (2025), our model predicts reductions in logical-error rates per unit time of up to $40\%$.
summary: This paper proposes an optimal strategy for scheduling syndrome measurements in quantum error-correcting memory, treating the measurement interval as an optimizable control parameter rather than a fixed clock cycle. By deriving that the optimal interval scales inversely with code distance ($\Delta t^* \propto 1/d$), the authors show this leads to an exponential suppression of logical errors. Furthermore, they introduce an adaptive timing protocol that significantly outperforms static scheduling when noise is bursty.
main_problem: The primary challenge is optimizing the syndrome-measurement timing ($\Delta t$) in quantum error-correcting codes to minimize logical errors by balancing accumulating idling noise against measurement-induced faults.
main_result: Optimal scheduling requires setting the interval inversely proportional to the code distance ($\Delta t^* \propto 1/d$), which yields an exponential reduction in logical error rates compared to fixed-interval protocols. Adaptive strategies further improve performance, especially during noise bursts.
method: The authors developed a phenomenological logical-noise model to analytically derive the optimal timing scaling and analyzed time-dependent noise using adaptive control theory.
model_or_system: The work focuses on fault-tolerant quantum memories implemented via rotated surface codes. The error sources modeled include idling errors (exponentially dependent on $\Delta t$) and measurement faults (linearly dependent on measurement frequency).
key_observables: Logical error rate ($p_L$), optimal syndrome interval ($\Delta t^*$), relative suppression factor ($\Gamma_{	ext{opt}}$), and the time-dependent noise activity $\lambda(t)$.
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), idling noise rate ($\lambda$), measurement fault probabilities ($p_{	ext{stab}}, p_{	ext{read}}$), and experimental parameters from Google's Willow device.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a phenomenological logical-noise model, and the adaptive strategy assumes instantaneous knowledge of the time-dependent noise profile $\lambda(t)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the trade-off between error sources vs. $\Delta t$, showing that $\Delta t \propto 1/d$ yields exponentially lower errors than constant intervals; other figures compare fixed vs. adaptive protocols for dynamic noise.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the fundamental trade-off, derives the optimal scaling $\Delta t^* \propto 1/d$, and then extends this analysis to time-dependent noise using an adaptive control strategy, concluding with quantitative predictions based on current experimental hardware parameters.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial theoretical guidance for designing next-generation quantum memories by moving beyond fixed operational cycles. The focus on optimizing the measurement schedule itself is a key area in open quantum systems and fault tolerance theory.
